{{DISPLAYTITLE:Chronology}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}
A timeline of Lean and of the work it grew from, from Automath to October 2026.

Every entry is stated, with its source, on the page named in its last column, and this page
adds nothing to those pages. Dates are of first statement, first publication or first
version, as the entry says. The dates of Lean's versions are those of its version
notes.<ref name="relnotes">''The Lean Language Reference'', "Release Notes", list of versions
with their dates (read 14 October 2026). https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/</ref>
Where a page gives two dates for one event, both are given here.

== Before Lean: 1966 to 2012 ==

{| class="wikitable"
! date !! event !! page
|-
| 1966 or 1967 || '''Automath''' conceived by N. G. de Bruijn at Eindhoven; his own accounts give 1966 and early 1967 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| Dec 1968 || De Bruijn presents the Automath language at the Symposium on Automatic Demonstration, Versailles; printed 1970 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| 1969 || Dana Scott devises the logic for computable functions that LCF is named after; his manuscript is published in 1993 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| 1971 || Per Martin-Löf's first type theory, an unpublished preprint, with a type of all types || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 1971 to 1976 || I. Zandleven writes most of Automath's checking programs || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| 1972 || Jean-Yves Girard's thesis shows a type of all types contradictory; Martin-Löf replaces it by a universe of small types (paper published 1998) || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 1972 || De Bruijn proposes writing bound variables as numbers, the '''de Bruijn indices''' Lean's terms still use || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| May 1972 || Robin Milner's report on '''Stanford LCF''' || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| c. 1973 || Milner begins Edinburgh LCF: a protected type of theorems, and tactics || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| Jul 1973 || Martin-Löf at the Logic Colloquium, Bristol: a hierarchy of universes and an identity type; printed 1975 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 1974 || The name '''proof irrelevance''' appears in an Automath report || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| 1976 || L. S. van Benthem Jutting's translation of Landau's ''Grundlagen der Analysis'' into Automath, in a five-volume report; his thesis 1977, published 1979 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| 1978 || ML, the metalanguage of LCF, described at the Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages; Milner's paper on polymorphic type inference || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| 1979 || ''Edinburgh LCF'', by Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| 1979 || Martin-Löf, "Constructive mathematics and computer programming", Hannover; the extensional theory; published 1982 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 1980 || De Bruijn's survey of the Automath project || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| Jun 1980 || Martin-Löf's Padua lectures, published in 1984 as ''Intuitionistic Type Theory'' || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 1983 to 1985 || The first type checker for the Theory of Constructions, mostly Gérard Huet's work || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| Jun 1984 || Coquand and Huet present a preliminary version of the calculus at Sophia-Antipolis || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 31 Jan 1985 || Thierry Coquand defends his thesis on the Theory of Constructions || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| c. 1985 || Cambridge LCF, by Lawrence Paulson; described in his book of 1987 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| 1986 || Nuprl, a proof assistant for an extensional type theory, described in a book; Martin-Löf recasts his theory in a logical framework || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| May 1986 || '''The Calculus of Constructions''', under that name, in an INRIA report; in ''Information and Computation'' 1988 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 1988 || Version 4.7 of the system later named Coq keeps its proof checker, the Constructive Engine, apart as a trusted core; HOL88 appears about the same year || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]], [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| 1989 || Inductive types added as primitives: the '''Calculus of Inductive Constructions''', by the Coq manual's date; the paper, presented at COLOG-88, is published in 1990 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| end of 1989 || The system is named Coq, with version 5.1 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 1991 || Milner receives the ACM Turing Award; the citation names LCF and ML || [[Lean theorem prover/History/LCF and the tactic idea|LCF and the tactic idea]]
|-
| 1993 || Christine Paulin-Mohring sets out the rules of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 1994 || ''Selected Papers on Automath''; the ALF proof editor || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]], [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 1995 || Antonius Hurkens publishes a simplified form of Girard's paradox || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|-
| 2002 || Freek Wiedijk's new Automath checker checks the ''Grundlagen'' translation in 0.6 seconds || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Automath|Automath]]
|-
| 2007 || Ulf Norell's thesis designs and implements a new Agda || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Martin-Löf type theory|Martin-Löf type theory]]
|}

== Lean 1 to Lean 3: 2013 to 2022 ==

{| class="wikitable"
! date !! event !! page
|-
| 2013 || '''Lean''' begun by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| 2013 || The ACM Software System Award goes to the team that first developed Coq || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 16 Jun 2014 || Lean 0.1, the first version || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| 2015 || '''"The Lean Theorem Prover (system description)"''', CADE-25, describing the version now called Lean 2 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| 2016 || Maryna Viazovska proves that the <math>E_8</math> lattice gives the densest sphere packing in eight dimensions || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Research mathematics|Research mathematics]]
|-
| 20 Jan 2017 || Lean 3.0.0 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| 2017 || Metaprogramming in Lean 3: tactics written in Lean itself || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| summer 2017 || '''mathlib''' begins, from the core library of Lean 3 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Mathlib and its community|Mathlib and its community]]
|-
| 2018 || Work on Lean 4 begins || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]]
|-
| 18 Jan 2019 || Lean 3.4.2, the last official version of Lean 3 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| 2019 || Mario Carneiro's account of Lean's type theory || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 26 Dec 2019 || Lean 3.5.0c, the first version maintained by the community || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| Jan 2020 || "The Lean Mathematical Library", by the mathlib Community, at CPP in New Orleans || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Mathlib and its community|Mathlib and its community]]
|-
| 5 Dec 2020 || Peter Scholze sets the '''Liquid Tensor Experiment''' challenge || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Liquid Tensor Experiment|The Liquid Tensor Experiment]]
|-
| early 2021 || Lean 4 made public || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]]
|-
| 2021 || '''"The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language"''', CADE-28 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]]
|-
| 2021 || The miniF2F benchmark of formal competition problems || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Machine learning and theorem proving|Machine learning and theorem proving]]
|-
| 28 May 2021 || The proof of Theorem 9.4, the one result Scholze had been worried about, is formalised || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Liquid Tensor Experiment|The Liquid Tensor Experiment]]
|-
| Dec 2021 || Plan for porting mathlib, then over 700,000 lines, to Lean 4 with Mathport || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]]
|-
| 14 Jul 2022 || The Liquid Tensor Experiment completed || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Liquid Tensor Experiment|The Liquid Tensor Experiment]]
|}

== Lean 4: 2023 to October 2026 ==

{| class="wikitable"
! date !! event !! page
|-
| 24 May 2023 || Lean 3.51.1c, the last community version of Lean 3 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]]
|-
| Jul 2023 || De Moura and Sebastian Ullrich found the '''Lean Focused Research Organization''' || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| 16 Jul 2023 || The port of mathlib to Lean 4 declared complete || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]]
|-
| 8 Sep 2023 || '''Lean 4.0.0''', the first stable version; a new version about every month follows || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]]
|-
| 9 Nov 2023 || Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao post their proof of the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture in characteristic 2 || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture|The polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture]]
|-
| 5 Dec 2023 || The formalisation of that proof is complete, three weeks after it began || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture|The polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture]]
|-
| Dec 2023 || Start of the Fermat's Last Theorem project, by the Lean FRO's timeline; announced April 2024 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]], [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The Fermat's Last Theorem project|The Fermat's Last Theorem project]]
|-
| Mar 2024 || Sidharth Hariharan and Viazovska begin formalising the eight-dimensional sphere packing || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Research mathematics|Research mathematics]]
|-
| 2024 || HepLean, later part of Physlib, begins || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Physics in Lean|Physics in Lean]]
|-
| Jul 2024 || Google DeepMind reports that AlphaProof, with a second system for geometry, reached silver-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Machine learning and theorem proving|Machine learning and theorem proving]]
|-
| 25 Sep 2024 || Terence Tao proposes the '''equational theories project''' || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The equational theories project|The equational theories project]]
|-
| Oct 2024 || The Fermat project's research council fellowship begins, to run until September 2029 || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The Fermat's Last Theorem project|The Fermat's Last Theorem project]]
|-
| Dec 2024 || Kevin Buzzard reports the problem met in a 1965 paper on divided powers sorted out, and the Fermat project back on track || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The Fermat's Last Theorem project|The Fermat's Last Theorem project]]
|-
| 12 Mar 2025 || Version 9.0 of the Rocq Prover completes the renaming of Coq || [[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]]
|-
| 14 Apr 2025 || The equational theories project reaches its primary goal: all 22,028,942 implications decided || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The equational theories project|The equational theories project]]
|-
| 2025 || Lean receives the ACM SIGPLAN Programming Languages Software Award; the 2015 system description receives the CADE Skolem Award || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| Jul 2025 || Gifts of $5 million each to the Lean FRO and to Mathlib announced, with a Mathlib Initiative to be set up || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Mathlib and its community|Mathlib and its community]]
|-
| 14 Aug 2025 || Lean 4.22.0: a new compiler, and the <code>grind</code> tactic || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| Nov 2025 || AlphaProof's method published in ''Nature'' || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Machine learning and theorem proving|Machine learning and theorem proving]]
|-
| Dec 2025 || The equational theories project's paper, with 34 authors || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The equational theories project|The equational theories project]]
|-
| Feb 2026 || The formal proof of sphere packing in dimension 8 completed, its final stages by an autoformalisation model || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Research mathematics|Research mathematics]]
|-
| Jul 2026 || Microsoft's SymCrypt code verified in Lean is in preview versions of Windows || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Software verification|Software verification]]
|-
| 22 Jul 2026 || Lean 4.32.1 fixes a soundness bug in the Lean kernel open to malicious metaprograms || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| 25 Jul 2026 || A false "disproof" of the Collatz conjecture, exploiting a bug in the Lean kernel, is published || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| 28 Jul 2026 || The exploit reduced to a short proof of <code>False</code> and reported; Lean 4.32.2 fixes it || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| Aug 2026 || A dataset of Lean statements of 50 theorems from the ''Annals of Mathematics'' announced || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Research mathematics|Research mathematics]]
|-
| 4 Sep 2026 || Anthropic announces a machine-written formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/The Fermat's Last Theorem project|The Fermat's Last Theorem project]]
|-
| Sep 2026 || The Lean FRO moves to six-month roadmaps, with independent checking planned as a routine step || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| 24 Sep 2026 || '''Lean 4.34.1''', the version with which this edition's code is checked || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| 12 Oct 2026 || Lean 4.35.0 || [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]
|-
| Oct 2026 || This wiki's framework for testing physical hypotheses is being restated in Lean, with Lean 4.34.1 pinned || [[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Principia Machina|Principia Machina]]
|}
